common_name: Jersey Gem Beach Plum (Rutgers-Bred Named Beach Plum Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a second, genetically distinct beach plum cultivar such as Hancock or Eastham for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained, salt-spray-exposed soil in full sun and site a second named beach plum cultivar nearby, since this species sets fruit poorly without a cross-pollinator. Jersey Gem is a beach plum selection bred by Rutgers University in New Jersey and singled out, alongside a small number of other named clones such as Resigno and ECOS, for producing larger and better-flavored fruit than typical unselected wild seedling stands, where fruit quality and sweetness vary considerably from bush to bush. Its purple-red to blue-black drupes ripen in late summer and are well suited to the traditional beach plum jams, jellies, and preserves long made along the Jersey Shore and greater mid-Atlantic coast. As a true dune-adapted shrub, it tolerates salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soils that would stress most other fruiting plants, needing only light pruning after bloom to stay productive.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station
Cornell University Cooperative Extension beach plum research

common_name: Resigno Beach Plum (Named Beach Plum Selection for Improved Fruit)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a second, genetically distinct beach plum cultivar for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Site in sandy, salt-spray-exposed, well-drained soil in full sun and plant beside a different named beach plum cultivar, since seedling beach plum and single clones set fruit poorly without a cross-pollinator. Resigno is one of a small group of named beach plum selections, along with Jersey Gem and ECOS, chosen from wild coastal populations for producing larger and better-flavored fruit than typical unimproved seedling stands, in which individual bushes can vary from sweet to notably sour or bitter. Its fruit ripens in late summer to shades of red, purple, or blue-black and is prized for the traditional New England and mid-Atlantic beach plum jams and jellies. As a true coastal dune native, it tolerates salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soil that would stress most other fruiting shrubs, and needs only light pruning after flowering to remain productive.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension beach plum research

common_name: ECOS Beach Plum (Named Beach Plum Selection for Improved Fruit)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a second, genetically distinct beach plum cultivar for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained, salt-spray-exposed soil in full sun with a second named beach plum cultivar nearby, since this species is only partially self-fertile and sets fruit poorly on its own. ECOS is one of a small group of named beach plum clones, alongside Jersey Gem and Resigno, selected for producing larger, better-flavored fruit than typical unimproved wild seedling stands, whose fruit quality is notoriously inconsistent from bush to bush. Its drupes ripen in late summer to red, purple, or blue-black and are traditionally used for jams, jellies, and preserves along the Atlantic coast from Cape Cod to the mid-Atlantic. As a true dune-adapted native shrub, it withstands salt spray, wind, and lean sandy soils that would stress or kill most other fruiting plants, and needs only light pruning after bloom to stay productive.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension beach plum research
